title: Parallel Scalability Limits
summary: Applying Amdahl's Law to real multicore scaling, the overheads the law itself ignores, and Gustafson's counterpoint.

slides.markdown:
Applying **Amdahl's Law** ([amdahls-law-fundamentals](amdahls-law-fundamentals)) to multicore scaling: if a fraction *s* of a program is inherently serial, speedup is capped at `1/s` no matter how many cores work the parallel remainder. A program that's 10% serial can never exceed 10x speedup — even with 1,000 cores on the other 90%.

This is why adding cores shows diminishing, then vanishing, returns: the serial fraction dominates total time as core count rises, since the parallel portion shrinks while the serial portion never does.

Amdahl's Law itself assumes the parallel portion runs at perfect efficiency — real code never does. **Synchronization overhead** — locks, barriers, atomic operations — eats into the theoretical speedup on top of the serial-fraction ceiling. Every thread that waits at a lock or barrier is doing zero useful work during that wait.

As core count grows, contention for shared locks typically gets *worse*, not better — more threads competing for the same critical section means more waiting, so the real-world speedup curve falls further below Amdahl's already-capped prediction as cores are added.

**Load imbalance** is a second real-world tax Amdahl's formula doesn't account for: if work is split unevenly across cores, the whole computation waits for the **slowest** core to finish, while the others sit idle after finishing early.

Even a perfectly parallelizable workload (in principle, 100% parallel) can scale badly in practice if the partitioning scheme hands some cores more work than others — the effective speedup is bounded by the busiest core's finish time, not the average.

![A speedup-vs-core-count curve flattening out, annotated with where Amdahl's ceiling, synchronization overhead, and load imbalance each bite](assets/speedup-curve.svg)

The curve rises steeply, then flattens as the serial fraction dominates a shrinking parallel portion (Amdahl), while synchronization and imbalance pull the real curve further below — most workloads plateau, or regress, before reaching the chip's full core count.

slides.markdown:
**Gustafson's Law** reframes the question: instead of "how much faster can I finish this *fixed* problem with more cores" (Amdahl's framing), it asks "how much *bigger* a problem can I solve in the same time?"

Here the serial fraction doesn't grow with problem size while the parallel portion does — scaling the problem *with* core count sidesteps Amdahl's ceiling. This matches real workloads: given 100x the cores, you don't run the same simulation 100x faster, you run a 100x more detailed one in the same time.

| | Amdahl's Law | Gustafson's Law |
|---|---|---|
| Problem size | Fixed | Scales with core count |
| Question asked | How much faster can this exact task finish? | How much more work fits in the same time? |
| Implication | Serial fraction caps speedup hard | Serial fraction's relative impact shrinks as problem scales |

**How to decide:** use Amdahl's framing for latency-bound tasks where the problem size truly can't grow (finishing one fixed job faster); use Gustafson's framing for throughput-bound tasks where more cores let you tackle a bigger problem in the same time (most scientific computing, big-data batch jobs) — the 'right' law depends entirely on which question your workload is actually asking.
